sections.title: Who They Are and Where They Lived About 1500
sections.text: The Inuit are the people of the far northern coasts. Their lands stretch from Alaska, across northern Canada, to Greenland. Each group has its own name. In northern Alaska they are the Iñupiat. In western Alaska and on the Russian side of the Bering Strait live the Yupik peoples, who are close cousins and speak related languages. Some Yupik prefer their own name to the word Inuit, and it is kind to use the name each people chooses. In Canada most call themselves Inuit, which means simply "the people." In Greenland the largest group are the Kalaallit. Their languages, Inupiaq, Inuktitut and Kalaallisut, belong to the Eskimo-Aleut family. They are close enough that a traveller can often follow a good part of what the others say. Their ancestors, whom scholars call the Thule people, began moving east from northern Alaska about AD 1000. Newer studies suggest the journey across Canada to Greenland happened very fast, and that most of it took place in the 1200s. By about 1500 Inuit families lived along almost every Arctic shore from Alaska to Greenland and Labrador. They lived in small groups of related families and moved with the seasons to wherever the animals would be. The winters were long and dark, and the sea froze for many months. Few people anywhere have made a home in such a cold place, and the Inuit did it with great skill, patience and care for one another.

sections.title: How They Lived and What They Ate
sections.text: Inuit families were some of the cleverest inventors in the world. Hunters went out in the kayak, a slim one-person boat with a covered top made of driftwood or bone and sealskin. Families and whaling crews used the umiak, a larger open skin boat. With a harpoon whose tip turned sideways inside the animal so it could not slip free, hunters took seals, walrus and, in some places, great whales. Inland in summer they hunted caribou, whose warm fur made the best winter clothing. In winter, teams of dogs pulled sleds across the ice. On the trail, a family could build a snow house, an igloo, in about an hour. At home many lived in sturdy houses of sod, stone and whalebone, partly dug into the ground to keep out the wind. A stone lamp burning seal oil, called the qulliq in Canada, gave light, warmth and heat for cooking. Women sewed waterproof boots and parkas so well that the stitches kept out icy water. Food came almost all from animals: seal, whale, caribou, fish and birds, with berries in the short summer. Much was eaten raw or frozen. Raw meat, fat and organs gave people vitamins they could not get from plants, because almost nothing green grows there. Sharing was the rule. When a hunter brought home a seal, the meat was shared out so no family went hungry. Children learned by watching and helping, and the elders were honoured for what they knew about ice, weather and animals.

sections.title: What They Believed About God, Creation, Spirits and the Dead
sections.text: Long before missionaries came, Inuit believed the whole world was alive with spirit. People, animals, the sea, the wind and even places had an inua, an inner spirit or soul. An animal let itself be caught by a hunter who showed it respect. So people followed careful rules to honour the animals they ate. A common custom was to give a freshly killed seal a drink of fresh water, because it had lived its life in salt water. One of the best-known spirit beings is the woman of the sea. Many in Canada call her Sedna, and other groups give her other names, such as Nuliajuk. In one common telling she was once a young woman who was thrown from a boat, and the sea animals came from her fingers. She lives at the bottom of the sea and keeps the seals, walrus and whales. When people broke the rules, she grew angry and held the animals back, and the people went hungry. There were also spirits of the sky and the weather, and the moon was sometimes a person in the stories. The shaman, called angakkuq, was a man or woman believed able to travel in spirit to the sea woman, comb her tangled hair and calm her, so the animals would return. Inuit believed a person's soul lived on after death. A person's name was thought to carry something of that person, so a baby named for someone who had died was welcomed as part of that loved one's life going on. Beliefs differed from place to place, and Inuit tell these stories in many ways.

sections.title: Their Ceremonies and Sacred Things
sections.text: Ceremonies helped keep a right relationship between people, animals and spirits. Many rules, or taboos, guarded the hunt. In some places, for example, land animals and sea animals had to be kept apart, and caribou skins were not to be sewn while people were hunting on the sea ice. After a death, families kept quiet days of mourning and avoided certain work, to show respect and keep the community safe. The shaman's séance was held in a darkened house. The angakkuq might be bound with cords, sing, and call helping spirits, while the people listened and sometimes confessed broken rules, so that the trouble could be put right. Drum dancing was, and still is, a great joy. A dancer holds a wide, flat drum made from a hoop covered with skin, and strikes the rim while singing songs. Some songs were funny or teasing, some told of a hunt, and some were passed down through families. In some places two people would sing teasing songs at each other, and this helped settle quarrels without fighting. In Alaska, big feasts honoured whales and the animals' spirits, and some Yupik communities held a festival to return the bladders of seals to the sea so the animals could be born again. The sharing of the catch was itself something close to sacred: the first seal of a boy, or the first whale of a season, was shared widely, teaching that a good hunter is a generous one. Amulets sewn into clothing were believed to give protection and strength.

sections.title: Their History Since the First Europeans Came
sections.text: Norse settlers from Iceland reached Greenland about AD 985 and lived there for several centuries. Inuit and Norse met there in the centuries that followed, sometimes trading and sometimes in conflict. The Norse farms were empty by the 1400s, while the Inuit stayed. In 1721 a Lutheran minister from Norway and Denmark, Hans Egede, came to Greenland to teach Christianity. Moravian missionaries later went to Greenland and Labrador, and Anglican, Catholic, Moravian and Russian Orthodox missions reached Canada and Alaska. Whalers came in the 1800s, bringing trade goods, but also diseases that took many lives. In 1845 the British explorer Sir John Franklin sailed into the Canadian Arctic with two ships, the Erebus and the Terror, and none of his men came home. Inuit saw the dying sailors and remembered what they saw. Their careful oral history helped searchers find the wreck of the Erebus in 2014 and the Terror in 2016. The 1900s were hard. In Canada many families were moved into towns, and children were sent away to schools far from home where they could not speak their language. In 1953 some families were moved far north to the High Arctic, and Canada later apologized for this in 2010. Inuit also worked hard for their rights. Alaska Natives reached a land settlement with the United States in 1971. Greenland gained home rule in 1979 and wider self-government in 2009. In 1993 Inuit in Canada signed a land claims agreement, and on April 1, 1999, the territory of Nunavut, meaning "our land," was born.

sections.title: The People Today
sections.text: Today about 180,000 Inuit live in four countries: Canada, Greenland, the United States in Alaska, and Russia. In Canada about 70,000 Inuit live mostly in four regions they call Inuit Nunangat, the Inuit homeland. In Greenland, Kalaallit and other Inuit are most of the people, and Kalaallisut is the official language. Inuit from all four countries work together through the Inuit Circumpolar Council, founded in 1977, to speak for the Arctic and its people. Most Inuit today are Christian. Many attend Anglican, Catholic, Lutheran, Moravian, Pentecostal or other churches, and some keep older customs beside their faith, such as honouring the animals, sharing food, and naming babies after loved ones who have died. Families still hunt seal and caribou, often from snowmobiles and motorboats, with GPS and satellite phones in the pack. Many children learn in their own language at school, and elders teach young people to read the ice and sew skin clothing. Inuit artists are known around the world for their prints, carvings and throat singing. There are real challenges. Food that must be flown north is very costly, good housing can be scarce, and the warming climate is making the sea ice thinner and less safe. Inuit leaders are working on these problems with patience and strength. For families who believe that Heavenly Father gives people the knowledge to make tools so His work can go forward, the Inuit story is a gentle lesson. The kayak, the oil lamp and the satellite phone can all bless lives when they are used with care, respect and a willingness to share.

sections.title: Who the Cree Are and Where They Lived Around 1500
sections.text: The Cree people call themselves by names that mean, in their own language, something like "the people." On the plains the word is Nehiyawak. In the east, people use names like Eeyou or Iiyiyiu. The name "Cree" came later. It is a short form of a French word that came from what the neighbouring Ojibwe people called one Cree band near James Bay. Cree is part of the large Algonquian family of languages, so it is a cousin of Ojibwe, Innu and Blackfoot. Around the year 1500, before Europeans came, Cree families lived across a huge northern land of forest, lakes and rivers. This land stretched from the shores of James Bay and Hudson Bay westward through what are now Quebec, Ontario and Manitoba. Encyclopedias say the Cree first lived in a smaller part of this land. They spread much farther in the 1600s and 1700s, after they began trading furs and getting guns. In time some Cree bands reached Alberta and Great Slave Lake. People of the forest are often called Woodland or Swampy Cree. The Plains Cree moved out onto the open grasslands in the 1700s, after the horse came. Cree families have lived in the boreal forest for thousands of years. They knew every river bend, berry patch and animal trail. Children learned the land from their grandparents the way a child today learns the streets near home. To understand the Cree, a parent can start with this: they belonged to the land, and they belonged to each other.

sections.title: How They Lived and What They Ate
sections.text: In the forest, life followed the seasons. In winter, small groups of related families spread out across their hunting grounds. Big gatherings would have used up the animals in one place too quickly. Men hunted moose, caribou and beaver, and they set traps for smaller animals. Women did a great deal of the work. They cleaned and tanned hides, sewed clothing and moccasins, dried meat and fish, and gathered berries. In summer, families came together at lakes and river mouths. There they fished, visited, held marriages and ceremonies, and traded. They travelled by birchbark canoe on the water and by snowshoe and toboggan on the snow. Homes were cone-shaped lodges covered with bark or hides. Food came from the land: moose, caribou, beaver, rabbit, ducks, geese and many kinds of fish. In some southern places there was wild rice, and everywhere there were berries such as blueberries and saskatoons. When the English Hudson's Bay Company began trading on Hudson Bay in 1670, the Cree became some of its most important partners. They brought furs and guided traders. They also passed European goods along to peoples farther inland. On the prairies, the Plains Cree used horses to hunt buffalo. They made pemmican, which is dried meat pounded with fat and berries. It kept for a long time and fed both families and fur traders. A child might like to know that a good hunter was honoured most for sharing. Meat was given to elders, widows and anyone in need.

sections.title: What They Believed About God, Creation, Spirits and the Dead
sections.text: Traditional Cree belief speaks of Kitchi Manitou (also spelled Kihci-manitow), the Great Spirit, who is above all. Cree teachers explain that the whole world is alive with spirit. Animals, waters, winds and special places all deserve respect. A hunter thanked the animal that gave its life. He treated its bones with care, believing that respect kept a right relationship between people and the animals that fed them. Many Cree stories are about Wisahkecahk (also written Wisakedjak). He is a trickster and helper, sometimes wise and sometimes foolish. His stories teach children what happens when people are greedy or proud. In one well-known Cree story, a great flood covers the world. Wisahkecahk sends animals diving for mud. The little muskrat brings some up, and from it a new earth is made. Young people, often around the time they became adults, went alone to fast and pray. They hoped to receive a vision and a spirit helper to guide their lives. Cree families have also kept a strong bond with those who have died. Feasts honour those who have passed on, and food is set aside for them. Prayers remember the ancestors as still part of the family. Latter-day Saint parents may notice a few things that feel familiar: love for a Creator above all, gratitude for daily food, fasting to seek guidance, and lasting ties to departed loved ones. It is best to let these beliefs stand in their own words, as the Cree describe them, and treat them with respect.

sections.title: Ceremonies and Sacred Things
sections.text: Cree ceremonies are holy to the people who keep them. Many details are shared only within the community, so families learning from outside should listen with respect. The sweat lodge is a small, low dome covered with hides or blankets. Inside, water is poured on hot stones to make steam while people pray and sing. It is a ceremony of cleansing and of starting fresh. The shaking tent is a tall, narrow lodge entered by a gifted spiritual leader. The Cree believe spirit helpers come there to give guidance and news from far away, and the tent moves when they arrive. The pipe is one of the most sacred objects. When people smoke a pipe together, they are making their prayers and promises true before the Creator. Treaties with Canada were opened with the pipe. To the Cree, those agreements were sacred promises, not just papers. On the plains, the Sun Dance (often called the Thirst Dance by the Plains Cree) is a great summer gathering of prayer, fasting and sacrifice for the good of the whole people. Round dances, where everyone holds hands and moves in a circle, are held to honour those who have passed on and to bring people together. Sweetgrass, sage, eagle feathers and the drum are also treated with great care. A parent might help a child see that, as in our own faith, sacred things are approached with clean hands, quiet hearts and reverence.

sections.title: Their History Since the First Europeans Came
sections.text: From the 1600s, French and English fur traders reached Cree country. After 1670, the Hudson's Bay Company built posts on the bay, and Cree trappers, guides and families became central to the fur trade. Many Cree and European traders married, and their children helped begin the Métis people. The trade brought metal tools, cloth and guns. It also brought diseases like smallpox, which took many lives. In 1840, the Methodist missionary James Evans worked at Norway House, in what is now Manitoba, with Cree helpers. Together they made a writing system called syllabics, where each symbol stands for a sound. It was so easy to learn that many Cree could soon read the Bible and send letters on birchbark. It is still used today. As the buffalo disappeared in the 1870s, Plains Cree leaders signed treaties with Canada. Treaty 6 was signed in 1876 at Fort Carlton and Fort Pitt. Some leaders, like Big Bear, held out for better terms. During the hard times of 1885, there was fighting at places like Frog Lake and Cut Knife. Afterward, the chiefs Poundmaker and Big Bear were sent to prison. Poundmaker had worked for peace. In 2019, the Prime Minister of Canada officially cleared his name. For many years, Cree children were sent to residential schools, where many were punished for speaking their language. In 2022, Pope Francis came to Maskwacis, a Cree community in Alberta, to apologize for the Catholic Church's part in those schools. In 1975, the Cree of Quebec signed the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement after a struggle over a huge hydroelectric project.

sections.title: The Cree People Today
sections.text: Today the Cree are the largest First Nation in Canada. About 350,000 people say they are Cree. They live in hundreds of communities from Quebec to Alberta, and many live in cities like Edmonton, Saskatoon and Winnipeg. In northern Quebec, the Eeyou Istchee Cree Nation has its own regional government. It helps run schools, health care and land use for its communities. Across the prairies, First Nations guided by the treaties keep working to make sure those old promises are honoured. Cree is one of the most widely spoken Indigenous languages in Canada. Elders and teachers work hard to pass it on, because so many children once lost it in the schools. Communities run Cree language classes and immersion programs, radio stations, dictionaries and phone apps. Syllabics now appear on road signs and computer keyboards. Many Cree families still hunt, fish and trap in the seasons. They gather at powwows and round dances and teach their children the old stories. Many are also Christians, and some keep both church and traditional ways. Families who believe that Heavenly Father gives people new tools so His work can go forward may see that here gently. A writing system made with a missionary, and now smartphones and radio, are helping a people keep their own words and stories. The same tools that once crowded out the language are now helping bring it back. That is a quiet lesson a parent can share: tools themselves are not good or bad. What matters is how we choose to use them.

sections.title: Who the Dene are and where they lived about 1500
sections.text: The Dene, also called Athabaskans, are many nations who speak languages from one big family. The word Dene means "the people" in their own languages. Around the year 1500 they lived across a huge land of forests, lakes and rivers in what is now Alaska, the Yukon, the Northwest Territories and the northern parts of the Canadian provinces. Two great rivers ran through much of this land. The Yukon River flows west across Alaska, and the Mackenzie River flows north to the Arctic Ocean. The Dene were not one single tribe. They were many related peoples. Some of them are the Dënesųłiné (also called Chipewyan), the Tłı̨chǫ (Dogrib), the Slavey, the Sahtu Dene, the Gwich'in, and the Koyukon, Tanana and Ahtna peoples of Alaska. Each group had its own home country, its own way of speaking and its own leaders, but they understood that they were related. Their language family reaches much farther than the North. Long ago, before 1500, some Dene families walked south for many generations. Their children's children became the Navajo and Apache peoples of the American Southwest. Scholars have worked this out by comparing the languages. Words in Navajo and Apache are closely related to words still spoken by Dene families near the Arctic. Other relatives settled along the Pacific coast in Oregon and California. So when a child in Arizona and a child in the Yukon speak their grandparents' languages, they are using sister languages from one old family.

sections.title: How they lived and what they ate
sections.text: The northern land is beautiful, but the winters are long, dark and very cold. To live well there, the Dene had to know the land closely and move with the seasons. Families travelled in small groups to where the food would be. In some places great herds of caribou passed by each year, and people hunted them with bows, spears and fences made of brush that guided the animals. In the forests they hunted moose, which gave a great deal of meat and strong hides. Fish were just as important. People set nets and traps in the big lakes, such as Great Slave Lake and Great Bear Lake, and in the rivers, catching whitefish, trout and, in Alaska, salmon. They dried meat and fish so they would have food in winter. In summer, women and children picked blueberries, cranberries and cloudberries. The Dene were clever makers of tools. They made snowshoes for walking on deep snow, birchbark canoes and toboggans, nets woven from willow bark or sinew, and warm clothes of caribou and moose hide, often sewn with porcupine quills and later with beads. After traders came, many Dene also trapped beaver, marten and fox and traded the furs for metal tools, guns, cloth and tea. Families who believe that good tools come from Heavenly Father can see in snowshoes and canoes how people used what they had to care for one another in a hard land. Sharing was a rule of life. A hunter who brought home meat shared it, because everyone's survival depended on it.

sections.title: What they believed about God, creation, spirits and the dead
sections.text: Dene beliefs differ from nation to nation, but some ideas are shared widely. Many Dene speak of a Creator who made the world and gave the land and animals to the people. They also taught that spirits live in all living things: animals, the land, the water and the sky. Because of this, animals were treated with respect. Hunters took only what they needed, spoke of animals carefully, and put bones back in proper places. They believed that if animals were treated with respect, they would keep coming back to feed the people. Dene also speak of medicine power, which in the Dënesųłiné language is called inkonze. It is a gift of spiritual strength or help. Sometimes it came to a person in a dream or a vision, often to a young person who went alone on the land. Dene Elder George Blondin, from the Sahtu region, wrote that medicine power is a gift from the Creator. He also taught that it could be used to help people or to harm them, so it had to be used wisely. Many Dene nations tell stories of a great traveller and teacher. In the Mackenzie country he is called Yamoria. People say he journeyed through the land, made dangerous giant animals smaller, and gave people laws for living well together. In Alaska, the Koyukon and other peoples tell many stories about Raven from the time when animals and people could talk. The Dene believed the spirit lives on after death. The dead were remembered with care, and families were careful to honour them so their spirits could rest.

sections.title: Ceremonies and sacred things
sections.text: The drum is at the heart of Dene gatherings. It is a round hand drum made of hide stretched over a wooden frame. Drummers stand together and sing while people dance. One well-loved dance is the tea dance, also called the round dance. Men, women and children join hands or stand shoulder to shoulder and move slowly in a large circle around the drummers, often all night at a big gathering. The circle reminds people that they belong together. Another beloved gathering is the hand game. Two teams face each other. One team hides small objects in their hands while their drummers beat and sing loudly. A player on the other team must guess which hand holds the object. It is exciting and loud, and whole communities come to watch. Today there are big hand game tournaments in the Northwest Territories and Yukon. Feasts are sacred too. When someone dies, the family and community gather to share food, to give gifts, and to remember the one who has gone. In Alaska, Athabascan peoples hold memorial potlatches, sometimes a year or more after a death. Families work for a long time to prepare food and gifts for everyone who comes. At some Dene gatherings, people make an offering to the fire. They put a little food or tobacco into the flames to give thanks and to remember the ancestors. When we teach our children about these ceremonies, we can treat them as gently and respectfully as we would want our own sacred things treated.

sections.title: Their history since the first Europeans came
sections.text: European traders reached Dene country in the 1700s. The Hudson's Bay Company and later the North West Company built trading posts. Dene trappers brought furs and received goods like metal pots, knives, guns, cloth and tea. Dene guides were very important to explorers. A Dënesųłiné leader named Matonabbee guided Samuel Hearne across the northern land between 1770 and 1772. In 1789 Alexander Mackenzie travelled down the great river that now carries his name, helped by Indigenous guides. The newcomers also brought sicknesses such as smallpox and measles, which took the lives of many Dene. In the 1800s Catholic and Anglican missionaries came, and many Dene became Christians while keeping much of their old way of life. When gold was found in the Klondike in the 1890s, thousands of miners rushed into Yukon land. Canada then signed treaties with the Dene: Treaty 8 in 1899 and Treaty 11 in 1921. Many Dene understood the treaties as promises of peace and friendship. They did not understand them as giving away their land. For many years, Dene children were sent to residential schools far from home, where they were often forbidden to speak their languages. Many suffered there, and families today are still healing. In the 1970s a large gas pipeline was planned along the Mackenzie Valley. Justice Thomas Berger travelled to Dene villages and listened to the people. In 1977 he recommended waiting ten years before building a pipeline so that land claims could be settled first. In Alaska, the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act of 1971 created Native corporations, including Doyon for the Athabascan Interior.

sections.title: The Dene people today
sections.text: Today Dene people live in towns and villages across the Northwest Territories, the Yukon, Alaska, and the northern parts of Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and British Columbia. Many also live in cities. In the Northwest Territories, the Dene Nation speaks for many Dene First Nations. Several Dene languages are official languages there, including Chipewyan, Tłı̨chǫ, North Slavey, South Slavey and Gwich'in. Some nations have signed modern agreements with Canada. The Gwich'in signed in 1992 and the Sahtu in 1993. The Tłı̨chǫ Agreement took effect in 2005 and gave the Tłı̨chǫ their own government over a large area of land. Many Yukon First Nations, most of them Athabaskan, have made self-government agreements too. In Alaska, the Tanana Chiefs Conference and other groups serve Athabascan villages along the Yukon and Tanana rivers. Many Dene families still hunt caribou and moose, set fishnets, pick berries and travel on the land. Now they also use snowmobiles, motorboats, radios and phones. Elders and teachers are working hard to keep the languages alive. They record stories, teach in schools, run culture camps, and make language apps for children. Dene leaders also work to protect the caribou, whose numbers have fallen in some herds, and to look after the rivers and land for children not yet born. Many Dene are Christians, and many keep the drum, the tea dance and the hand games as well. Families who believe the same tool can bless or harm may notice how Dene communities choose carefully, using new tools to carry old language, faith and respect forward.

sections.title: Who They Are and Where They Lived About 1500
sections.text: The Ojibwe call themselves Anishinaabe, a word often explained as the original people. Neighbors and governments have also called them Chippewa, and some groups are known as Saulteaux, a French name for the people near Sault Ste. Marie, and Mississauga in southern Ontario. Many Ojibwe today prefer their own name over Chippewa. Their language is Ojibwe, or Anishinaabemowin, part of the large Algonquian family of languages. They are close relatives of the Odawa and Potawatomi. Together the three peoples are sometimes called the Three Fires. Ojibwe elders tell a migration story. Long ago the people lived near the great salt water in the east. A sacred shell in the sky led them west in stages, stopping at several places along the way, until they reached the place where food grows on the water, which is wild rice. By about 1500 their ancestors were living along the shores of the Great Lakes, especially around Lake Huron and Lake Superior. By the 1600s, when French travelers first wrote about them, they were well settled there. Later they spread west into what are now Wisconsin and Minnesota and north into the forests of Ontario and Manitoba. Some went as far as North Dakota, Montana and Saskatchewan. It was a land of lakes, rivers, birch and pine forests, and long, snowy winters. Families had to know that land well to live in it, and they did.

sections.title: How They Lived and What They Ate
sections.text: Ojibwe life moved with the seasons. Families did not stay in one place all year. They went where the food was. In early spring, families went to their sugar bush, a grove of maple trees. They tapped the trees and boiled the sap down into maple sugar. People ate the sugar and used it to flavor food. In summer, families gathered in larger villages near lakes. They fished, picked berries, and in the warmer south grew corn, beans and squash. Late summer brought the wild rice harvest. Two people would go out in a birch-bark canoe. One pushed the canoe gently through the rice beds with a long pole. The other used two sticks to bend the stalks and knock the ripe grains into the boat. Wild rice, called manoomin, was and still is a sacred food. In fall and winter, smaller family groups spread out to hunt deer, moose and other animals and to trap. Homes were wigwams, dome-shaped lodges of bent poles covered with birch bark or woven mats, easy to build and move. Birch bark was a wonderful gift. It made canoes, containers, roofs and even scrolls for writing. When French traders came, the Ojibwe became central to the fur trade, trading beaver and other furs for metal kettles, knives, cloth and guns. Some of these new tools made life easier. Others, like alcohol and later the overhunting of animals, brought harm. This is a gentle reminder for families that the same tool can bless or harm, depending on how it is used.

sections.title: What They Believed About God, Creation, Spirits and the Dead
sections.text: The Ojibwe have long spoken of Gitchi Manitou, often translated as the Great Spirit or Great Mystery, the source of life. They believe the world is full of manidoog, spirits or living powers, in animals, plants, waters, winds and stones. So people tried to live with thankfulness and respect, taking only what they needed and giving thanks for it. Many stories tell of Nanabozho, also called Wenabozho. He is a teacher and trickster who is part spirit and part person. In some tellings, after a great flood, he helped make the earth again from a little mud brought up from under the water by a small muskrat. His stories are funny, wise and sometimes about mistakes, so children learn both what to do and what not to do. Elders also teach the Seven Grandfather Teachings, which are wisdom, love, respect, bravery, honesty, humility and truth. Ojibwe tradition teaches that a person's spirit lives on after death. Many families describe the soul taking a journey westward to a land of souls. Families traditionally held feasts and offered food and tobacco to honor those who had died, and in some places they built small wooden houses over graves. Beliefs differ between communities and families. Many Ojibwe today are Christian, many follow traditional ways, and many respectfully hold both. When teaching children, it is kind to say "many Ojibwe believe" rather than speaking for every person.

sections.title: Ceremonies and Sacred Things
sections.text: The Midewiwin, sometimes called the Grand Medicine Society, is a sacred society of healers and teachers. Its members learn about healing plants, right living and the history of the people. Its teachings were kept partly on birch-bark scrolls called wiigwaasabakoon. The scrolls use drawings and symbols to help trained keepers remember songs, ceremonies and migration routes. Because they are sacred, families should treat them with respect and not ask to see or copy them as if they were ordinary pictures. The Seven Fires prophecy was first taught among Midewiwin people. It was shared more widely by Ojibwe teacher Edward Benton-Banai in The Mishomis Book. Other sacred practices include the sweat lodge, a small domed lodge where heated stones and water make steam for prayer and cleansing. Naming ceremonies give a child a spirit name, often through an elder who prays and fasts to receive it. The drum is honored as having a heartbeat and is cared for by drum keepers. Tobacco, called asemaa, is offered in prayer, given when asking an elder for help or teaching, and laid down when taking something from the earth. In the twentieth century the Ojibwe also gave the jingle dress dance to the powwow world. It is a healing dance in which the dress is covered with rows of metal cones that ring softly. Many families also know the dreamcatcher, which began among the Ojibwe as a small web hung over a baby's cradle. Families who visit public powwows are welcome to watch respectfully and should listen to the announcer about when photographs are allowed.

sections.title: Their History Since the First Europeans Came
sections.text: French explorers reached Ojibwe lands in the early 1600s. Britannica gives the year as 1622. French priests and traders soon followed. The Ojibwe became important partners in the fur trade, and Sault Ste. Marie and Madeline Island in Lake Superior became great gathering places. With the trade came new goods, but also new diseases that took many lives. Over the 1700s the Ojibwe moved west, and there were long years of conflict with the Dakota, who lived in what is now Minnesota. After the British and then the United States and Canada took control of the region, the Ojibwe signed many treaties in the 1800s. Britannica notes that they were forced to sign a series of treaties with the United States. In these treaties they gave up huge areas of land, but they kept reservations, and in several treaties they kept the right to hunt, fish and gather rice on land they had given up. In Canada, treaties created reserves for Ojibwe First Nations. Later, many Ojibwe children were sent to boarding schools in the United States and residential schools in Canada. There they were often punished for speaking their own language, and many families still feel that sorrow. Through all of this the Ojibwe held on. They kept their families, their stories and their rice lakes, and they stood up for their treaty rights in courts. In 1999 the United States Supreme Court upheld the hunting, fishing and gathering rights of several bands under an 1837 treaty.

sections.title: The People Today
sections.text: The Ojibwe are one of the largest Native peoples north of Mexico. Britannica reports that the 2020 United States census counted more than 130,000 people of Ojibwe descent. It also reports that more than 92,000 people in Canada said they had Ojibwe ancestry in the 2021 census. Together that is well over 200,000 people. They live in many self-governing bands and First Nations. In the United States these are spread across Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota, North Dakota and Montana. In Canada they stretch from Quebec and Ontario across Manitoba and Saskatchewan. Many also live in cities such as Minneapolis, Winnipeg and Toronto. Ojibwe people work as teachers, nurses, lawyers, artists, business owners, soldiers and leaders. Families still harvest wild rice, make maple sugar and fish the lakes. Communities are working hard to care for the rice beds and waters. Learning the language again is one of the most hopeful parts of Ojibwe life today. Some schools teach children entirely in Ojibwe. The University of Minnesota keeps a free online Ojibwe People's Dictionary with recordings of fluent speakers, so anyone can hear the words spoken. Here families can see a lovely example of how tools like computers, recordings and the internet can help a good work go forward, as birch-bark scrolls once did. Powwows, ceremonies, storytelling and beadwork are alive and growing. A child might learn to say boozhoo, a common Ojibwe greeting, and miigwech, which means thank you.

sections.title: What Has Been Connected with Israel, the Book of Mormon or a Visiting Teacher
sections.text: There is no Ojibwe tradition of a visiting white god or a bearded teacher from across the sea. The Seven Fires prophecy is sometimes mentioned in these talks because it tells of a light-skinned people coming from the east, with a warning to choose the right road. But in Ojibwe teaching this is a prophecy about newcomers and the choices of all peoples. It is not a story about a god or a holy visitor, and it should not be retold as one. The clearest record of an Israel connection comes from William Whipple Warren. Warren was the son of an Ojibwe mother and a white father, and he wrote History of the Ojibway People around 1852. It was published by the Minnesota Historical Society in 1885. Like many writers of his time, Warren thought the Ojibwe were probably descended from a portion of the ten lost tribes of Israel. He pointed to things he saw as similar, such as the clan system and religious customs. Later scholars value Warren for saving many Ojibwe oral traditions. However, a scholarly review of his book notes that his history cannot be accepted unquestioningly, because he shaped Ojibwe history to fit the Christian views of his day. The lost tribes idea is not an Ojibwe teaching. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints teaches that the Book of Mormon peoples are among the ancestors of the American Indians. The Church has not named the Ojibwe or any particular nation as their descendants. It also teaches that the Americas held many other peoples whose history we do not fully know.

sections.title: Who the Tlingit Are and Where They Lived About 1500
sections.text: The Tlingit are a people of the far northwest corner of North America. In their own language, which they call Lingít, the name means something like "people." Around the year 1500 they lived along the green, rainy coast and islands of what is now southeast Alaska. Their land ran from about Yakutat Bay in the north down to the area near today's Canadian border in the south. It was a land of deep forests, tall mountains, glaciers and many waterways. Families had lived there for thousands of years. The Tlingit did not have one king. Instead they lived in a number of local communities, each with its own winter villages, rivers, bays and hunting grounds. A village was a row of big wooden plank houses facing the water, with canoes pulled up on the beach in front. Each house was home to several related families, often more than twenty or thirty people. Every Tlingit person belonged to one of two great halves of the people, called moieties: the Raven and the Eagle, which some families call the Wolf. You belonged to your mother's side, not your father's. Inside each moiety were clans, and inside each clan were house groups. Each clan had its own history, its own names and its own crests. A child grew up knowing which clan they belonged to, which house they came from, and how they were related to everyone else in the village.

sections.title: How They Lived and What They Ate
sections.text: The sea and the rivers gave the Tlingit almost everything they needed. Every summer, huge runs of salmon swam up the streams, and families worked together to catch them with traps, weirs and nets. They dried and smoked the fish so there would be plenty to eat all winter. They caught halibut in deep water using carved wooden hooks. In spring they netted eulachon, a small oily fish, and boiled it down into a rich oil that people ate with many foods, much as we might use butter. Men hunted seals, sea lions and sea otters from canoes, and on land they hunted deer and mountain goats. Women and children gathered berries, roots, clams and seaweed, and dried them to keep. Giant red and yellow cedar trees were a great gift. From one huge cedar log, skilled carvers could make a seagoing canoe. Cedar planks became houses, and cedar was carved into boxes, bowls, masks and tall poles. Weavers made the famous Chilkat blankets from mountain goat wool and cedar bark, woven with clan designs. The Tlingit were also great traders. They paddled long distances along the coast and walked mountain trails to trade with peoples living far inland, carrying fish oil, shells and finished goods and bringing back furs, copper and other things. Because food was plentiful when people worked hard in summer, winter was a time for stories, art and gatherings. Parents can point out how much this way of life depended on knowing the land well and sharing the work.

sections.title: What They Believed About Creation, Spirits and the Dead
sections.text: The best-known figure in Tlingit stories is Raven. Raven is clever, hungry and often a trickster who gets into trouble, but he also shapes the world. One famous story tells how long ago the world was dark, because a rich old man kept the sun, moon and stars locked away in boxes in his house. Raven turned himself into a tiny thing, was born as the old man's grandson, and cried and cried until his grandfather let him play with the boxes. Then Raven let the light out, and the world has had daylight ever since. Tlingit people also believed that the world is full of spirits, called yéik, and that animals, fish, trees and even the mountains and glaciers deserve respect. A hunter or fisher thanked the animals and treated their remains carefully, so the animals would keep coming back. Some people were shamans, called ixt', who were believed to have spirit helpers. The shaman's work was to heal the sick, look into the future and protect the people. The Tlingit believed that a person's spirit goes on after death. Many believed that people could be born again into their own clan, so a grandchild might be seen as someone who had come back. In older times the dead were cremated, and their ashes and belongings were cared for by the clan. When teaching a child, a parent can explain that these are a people's sacred stories, to be spoken of with respect, and that many Tlingit families today also hold Christian faith alongside love for these old teachings.

sections.title: Ceremonies and Sacred Things
sections.text: The most important Tlingit gathering is often called a potlatch in English, though Tlingit people call the great memorial gathering a koo.éex'. It is usually held about a year or more after someone has died. The clan of the person who died invites guests from the opposite moiety, the people who helped them during their time of sorrow by caring for the body and comforting the family. The hosts feed their guests, sing, dance, give speeches and give away gifts to say thank you. Raising a new house or a new pole could also be marked with this kind of ceremony. These gatherings were how the people mourned, healed, paid their debts of kindness and showed that the clan was still strong. Clan crests are another sacred part of Tlingit life. A crest might be an animal, such as a frog, a bear, a killer whale or a raven, linked to an event in the clan's history. Crests were carved on poles and house posts and woven into blankets and robes. Special clan treasures are called at.óow, which means "owned things." They can be robes, hats, songs, names, stories or even places, and they were often paid for by the lives or great efforts of ancestors. An at.óow belongs to the whole clan, not to one person, and it is brought out with care at ceremonies. Totem poles could honor a person who had died, tell a clan story or welcome visitors. For a child, these can be compared to the way families keep heirlooms and records to remember those who came before.

sections.title: Their History Since the First Europeans Came
sections.text: In the 1700s, Russian, Spanish, British and later American ships began to arrive on the Tlingit coast, wanting furs, especially sea otter skins. Trade brought new goods, but also new sicknesses such as smallpox, which took many lives. In 1799 Russian traders built a post near the Tlingit village of Shee Atika, on the island now called Baranof Island. In 1802 Tlingit warriors attacked the Russian post, called Redoubt Saint Michael, and killed nearly all of the Russians and Aleut workers there. In late September 1804 the Russians came back with ships and demanded that the Kiks.ádi clan give up their village. The Tlingit moved to a wooden fort and defended it, and on October 1 the Russian ship Neva and other ships fired on it. After several days the Tlingit left the fort and walked across the mountains to safety. The Russians then built the town of New Archangel, later called Sitka, on the old village site. The National Park Service says this 1804 battle was the end of open Tlingit resistance, but the Russians stayed watchful. In 1867 the United States bought Alaska from Russia, even though the Tlingit had never sold their land. Many Tlingit had joined the Russian Orthodox Church, and later Presbyterian and other missions came. Children were sent to schools where they were often punished for speaking Lingít. In 1912 Tlingit and other Native people helped found the Alaska Native Brotherhood, and soon after the Alaska Native Sisterhood, to work for fair treatment. A Tlingit woman named Elizabeth Peratrovich spoke boldly and kindly before the territorial lawmakers, and in 1945 Alaska passed a law against discrimination.

sections.title: The Tlingit People Today
sections.text: Today about 17,000 people are Tlingit, and many still live in southeast Alaska in towns such as Juneau, Sitka, Yakutat, Hoonah, Angoon, Kake and Klawock, as well as in Canada and across the United States. Tlingit people work as teachers, fishers, carvers, nurses, lawyers, leaders and much more. For many years the Tlingit and Haida worked together in the courts to be paid for land that had been taken. The Central Council of Tlingit and Haida Indian Tribes of Alaska, based in Juneau, grew out of that effort, and the United States Congress confirmed it as a federally recognized tribe by a law passed in 1994. In 2025 the tribe described itself as having more than 38,000 citizens, counting Tlingit and Haida people together. In 1971 a law called the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act settled many land claims, and Sealaska, a company owned by Native people of southeast Alaska, was formed. Families still hold memorial gatherings, still wear clan robes, and still introduce themselves by their moiety, clan and house. Carvers raise new totem poles, and weavers again make Chilkat and Ravenstar robes. The Lingít language has only a small number of elders who learned it as their first language, so families, schools and the tribe are working hard to teach it to children again, including in a Lingít language preschool run by the tribe. Sitka National Historical Park keeps the 1804 battle site, and in 2020 archaeologists reported finding traces of the Tlingit fort. Parents can share with children that this is a living people, carefully passing what they love on to their grandchildren, as all good families hope to do.

sections.title: Who the Haida Are and Where They Lived About 1500
sections.text: The Haida are a people of the sea who live on Haida Gwaii, a group of more than one hundred and fifty islands off the north coast of what is now British Columbia, Canada. For many years outsiders called these islands the Queen Charlotte Islands. The Haida call their home Haida Gwaii, which means islands of the people. Archaeology shows that people have lived on these islands for at least 13,000 years. Haida families say their people have been there since the beginning of their own history. In about the year 1500, Haida villages lined the beaches of the islands. Each village had a row of big cedar plank houses facing the water, with carved poles standing in front. Every Haida person belonged to one of two large family groups, called Raven and Eagle. A child joined the group of their mother, not their father, and a Raven was expected to marry an Eagle. Some Haida families later moved north across the water to the southern part of Prince of Wales Island in what is now Alaska. These people are called the Kaigani Haida. They probably settled there a few hundred years ago, after 1500, and their descendants still live in Alaska today, mostly in the town of Hydaburg. The Haida language is called an isolate. That means it is not related to any other language in the world that we know of. It had a northern way of speaking, used at Masset and in Alaska, and a southern way of speaking, used at Skidegate. Today only a few elders grew up speaking it as their first language, so Haida families are working hard to teach it to children again.

sections.title: How They Lived and What They Ate
sections.text: The Haida were master canoe builders. They cut down giant red cedar trees and hollowed them out by hand to make dugout canoes. Some were small fishing boats. Others were great ocean canoes long enough to carry many paddlers and heavy loads. Haida canoes were so well made that people on the mainland traded valuable goods to get them. With these canoes the Haida traveled far along the coast to trade, visit, and sometimes go to war. The sea fed them well. Salmon came up the streams every year, and families caught many and dried or smoked them to eat in winter. Men fished for halibut, a huge flat fish, with carved wooden hooks far out in the deep water. They hunted seals, sea lions and sea otters. Women and children gathered seaweed, clams, shellfish, bird eggs, roots and many kinds of berries. Cedar trees gave them almost everything else they needed. The wood made houses, boxes, bowls and canoes. The soft inner bark was woven into clothing, mats, hats and baskets. Spruce roots were woven into hats so tight they kept out the rain. In a big Haida house, several related families lived together around a central fire. The chief of the house was honored, and each family knew its place and its duties. Summer was the busy time of fishing and gathering. Winter was the time for staying in the villages, telling stories, carving, and holding feasts. Children learned by watching and helping their parents and grandparents. Families who believe our Father in Heaven gives people skill and knowledge can see here a people who used wonderful skill to care for their families and live well with the land and sea.

sections.title: What They Believed About Creation, Spirits and the Dead
sections.text: The Haida have many sacred stories that elders passed down by voice, long before they were written. One of the best known is about Raven. In the stories, Raven is clever, hungry and often tricky. Long ago the world was dark, and Raven stole the light, the sun, moon and stars, from a chief who kept them hidden in boxes, and so light came into the world. In another story, Raven found a large clamshell on a beach. Small frightened beings were hiding inside it. Raven coaxed them out, and they became the first people. The Haida artist Bill Reid carved this story in a famous large wooden sculpture called The Raven and the First Men, which is kept at the Museum of Anthropology at the University of British Columbia. The Haida believed the world was full of beings with power. There were supernatural beings in the sea, such as killer whales who lived in houses under the water, and beings of the forest and the mountains. Animals were thought to be like people in their own way, and hunters showed them respect. Special healers called shamans were believed to speak with the spirit world, heal the sick, and help the people. The Haida also believed that a person who died could be born again into their own family, so a new baby might be recognized as a grandparent returning. When we teach children about the beliefs of another people, we can speak of them with respect, as treasured stories that carry a people's history, values and sense of the sacred, just as we treasure our own.

sections.title: Ceremonies and Sacred Things
sections.text: The most important Haida gathering was the potlatch. A potlatch was a large feast where a family invited many guests, fed them, and gave them gifts. It was held to mark big moments, such as raising a new house, giving a person a new name, or honoring a chief who had died and naming the one who would take his place. The guests acted as witnesses. By accepting gifts and food, they agreed that what had happened was true and right. In this way a potlatch was a bit like a public record, kept in the memory of the people instead of on paper. There were songs, dances, speeches and masks. Carved poles were a large part of Haida life. Many people call them totem poles. A pole in front of a house showed the crests of the family who lived there, such as Raven, Eagle, Bear, Killer Whale or Frog, and told who they were and where they came from. Some poles were part of the house itself, with a doorway cut through the bottom. A special kind called a mortuary pole was made for a high chief who had died. The chief's remains were placed in a box near the top of the pole, high above the village, as a sign of great honor. A memorial pole was raised to remember a person without holding their remains. For many years, from 1884 until 1951, the government of Canada made potlatches against the law. Haida families kept as much of their culture as they could, and today potlatches and pole raisings are held again, with joy.

sections.title: History Since the First Europeans Came
sections.text: The first known meeting between the Haida and Europeans came in 1774, when a Spanish ship led by Juan Pérez sailed near the north end of Haida Gwaii. Haida people paddled out in canoes to trade with the sailors. In 1787 a British trader, George Dixon, named the islands the Queen Charlotte Islands, after the wife of the British king. Soon many ships came to buy sea otter furs, which sold for high prices in China. The Haida were skilled and careful traders, and for a time they grew wealthy. In those years Haida carvers made more great poles than ever before. Some artists also began carving argillite, a soft black stone found only on Haida Gwaii, into small figures, plates and pipes that visitors bought. Haida poles and argillite carvings are counted among the finest art of North America. Then came great sorrow. In 1862 smallpox, a terrible disease, spread from the town of Victoria up the coast. The Haida had no protection from it, and it killed most of the people. Other diseases followed. By around 1900 only a few hundred Haida were left. Many villages were left empty, and the survivors moved together into two towns, Masset and Skidegate. Christian missionaries came in the 1870s and 1880s, and many Haida joined their churches. Children were later sent away to residential schools, where they were often not allowed to speak Haida. Many poles were cut down or taken to museums far away. Even through all this loss, the Haida remembered who they were. The old village of SGang Gwaay, with its standing poles, was named a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 1981.

sections.title: The Haida People Today
sections.text: Today the Haida are a strong and living people. Most live in the towns of Old Massett and Skidegate on Haida Gwaii, in Hydaburg and nearby places in Alaska, and in cities across Canada and the United States. The Council of the Haida Nation is their own government. In the 1980s Haida people stood peacefully on Lyell Island to protect the old forests from logging. This led to an agreement in 1993 with Canada to protect the southern islands together, in a place now called Gwaii Haanas, which the Haida and Canada manage as partners. In 2010 the name Queen Charlotte Islands was officially set aside, and the islands are now called Haida Gwaii. In 2024 the Haida Nation and the province of British Columbia signed an agreement called the Rising Tide Haida Title Lands Agreement. In it, British Columbia formally recognized that the Haida Nation holds Aboriginal title, a kind of ownership right, throughout Haida Gwaii, and the two governments began moving decisions about the land over to the Haida Nation step by step. Haida art is flourishing again. In 1969 the artist Robert Davidson raised a new carved pole in Old Massett, the first one raised there in many decades, and many artists have followed. The Haida Heritage Centre at Kay Llnagaay near Skidegate welcomes visitors and teaches young people. Elders and teachers work together to save the Haida language, recording the speech of the last fluent speakers and teaching it in schools. The Haida story shows how a people can heal and grow strong after great loss. Families who believe that tools and knowledge come from Heavenly Father may notice that recordings, books and computers, which can be used for good or harm, are now helping the Haida keep their own words alive for their grandchildren.

sections.title: Who They Are and Where They Lived
sections.text: The Kwakwaka'wakw are a people of the Pacific coast of Canada, in what is now British Columbia. Their name means "those who speak Kwak'wala." It shows that what ties the people together is their shared language, which has several dialects. Older books call them the Kwakiutl, and you will still see that name in museums. Around the year 1500 their families lived along the coast of northern Vancouver Island, on the many small islands nearby, and in the deep, quiet inlets of the mainland across the water. This is a land of tall cedar and spruce forests, misty mountains, cold clear rivers and a sea full of life. People had already lived here for thousands of years. The Kwakwaka'wakw were not one kingdom with one ruler. They were a family of separate tribes, about seventeen in older times, and each had its own villages and chiefs. Each tribe was made up of smaller family groups called 'namima. Each 'namima traced its beginning to one first ancestor and kept its own names, songs, stories and crests. Villages were usually built on a beach facing the water, with a row of big houses looking out to sea, because the sea was their road, their food store and their neighbour. Children grew up knowing which family they belonged to, which names they might one day carry, and which places along the shore belonged to their people.

sections.title: How They Lived and What They Ate
sections.text: The Kwakwaka'wakw lived mostly from the sea and the rivers. Their most important food was salmon. Every year the salmon swam up the rivers in great numbers, and families caught them with traps, weirs and nets, then dried and smoked them so there would be food all winter. In spring came the eulachon, a small, oily fish. Its oil was boiled out and kept in boxes as a rich food and a valued gift. People also fished for halibut and cod in deeper water, gathered clams and other shellfish on the beaches, and hunted seals, deer and mountain goats. Women and children picked many kinds of berries in summer, along with roots and green shoots. Berries were often dried into cakes so they would keep. The red cedar tree was almost as important as the salmon. From its straight wood, men split long planks to build large houses where several related families lived together, each with its own fire. From single huge cedar logs they carved canoes, some big enough to carry many people far along the coast. Cedar bark was pulled into strips and woven into clothing, mats, baskets and rope. Cedar wood was also steamed and bent into watertight boxes for storing food and treasures. Summer was a busy time of moving to fishing and gathering camps. Winter was a time to stay in the big villages, live on stored food, and turn to ceremonies and stories.

sections.title: What They Believed About Creation, Spirits and the Dead
sections.text: The Kwakwaka'wakw understood the world as full of living powers. People, animals, birds, sea creatures, trees and even the weather all had spirit and deserved respect. Each family's history began with a first ancestor who, long ago, came down from the sky, up from the sea, or out of the earth in the form of an animal or bird, such as Thunderbird or a creature of the sea. In these stories the ancestor took off the animal form and became human, and then founded the family and its first village. This is why families carry animal crests, and why a mask can open to show a human face inside. The stories also tell of beings who changed the world in early times and set it in order for people. The year was divided in two. In summer, life was ordinary and busy with food gathering. In winter the spirits were believed to be close, and that was the season for the most sacred ceremonies. People showed thanks to the salmon and other animals that gave their lives for food, and took care not to waste or mistreat them. They believed the dead went on to another world. In older times the dead were often laid to rest in wooden boxes, which were sometimes placed in trees, in caves or on small islands set apart. In the 1800s and 1900s many Kwakwaka'wakw also became Christians, and today many families hold both their faith and their old family traditions with great care.

sections.title: Ceremonies and Sacred Things
sections.text: The best-known Kwakwaka'wakw ceremony is the potlatch. A potlatch is a large gathering in the big house, hosted by a family to mark an important event. It might be the giving of a name, a marriage, raising a memorial pole, or honouring someone who has died. Guests come as witnesses. The host family shows its songs, dances and masks, tells its history, and gives gifts to everyone present. By accepting the gifts, the guests agree that what happened is true and right, a little like signing a record, but written in people's memories. In this way the potlatch was their government, their courtroom and their history book all in one. Canada made the potlatch against the law from 1885 to 1951, but many families kept holding it in secret. The winter ceremonies also included the Hamatsa, the most important of the secret dance societies. In this dance a young person is seen as being carried off by a wild, fearsome spirit of the far north, and is then slowly calmed and brought back into the community through songs and dances. Huge bird masks with long beaks clatter and snap, and some masks open on hidden strings to show a second face inside. This is the transformation masks are famous for. Other treasured things include coppers, which are large shield-shaped plates of copper of great value, carved house posts and totem poles, painted screens, button blankets, and the family songs and names, which are held to be just as precious as anything you can touch.

sections.title: Art, Masks and the Big House
sections.text: Kwakwaka'wakw art is known around the world for its bold colours, deep carving and sense of movement. Their carvers make masks, feast dishes, rattles, house posts and tall poles that show family crests such as Thunderbird, Killer Whale, Raven, Wolf and Bear. A pole is not something to worship. It is more like a family tree or a history sign, telling everyone who the family is and where it came from. Many masks were made to be seen by firelight in the big house, where moving shadows and the turning of the dancer made them seem alive. Some masks are made in two or three layers. When the dancer pulls a cord, the outer face of a bird or animal opens to show a human face inside. This shows the old teaching that ancestors once moved between animal and human form. Learning to carve was passed from master to apprentice, often within families. In the 1900s, carvers such as Mungo Martin kept these skills alive during the years when the potlatch was banned. He later taught younger artists, who in turn taught others. The big house itself is sacred space. It is a large cedar building with a dirt floor and a central fire, where families gather, guests are seated by rank, and dances come in from behind a painted screen. Today new big houses stand in several communities, and parents and grandparents bring children there to watch, listen and learn.

sections.title: History Since the Europeans Came
sections.text: European ships began sailing along this coast in the late 1700s, and trade in sea otter furs and other goods followed. In 1849 the Hudson's Bay Company built a trading post called Fort Rupert in Kwakwaka'wakw territory, and the town grew into a meeting place for many families. Contact also brought great sorrow. Diseases such as smallpox, which the people had never met before, spread quickly, especially in the 1860s. Their numbers fell sharply between about 1830 and 1880. Missionaries came, and many people became Christians. Government officials later set up reserves and residential schools. One was St. Michael's at Alert Bay, where children were sent away from their families and often discouraged from speaking Kwak'wala. In 1885 Canada banned the potlatch. In 1921 a large potlatch was held by Dan Cranmer at Village Island. Afterward many people were arrested, and some were sent to jail. To win their freedom, families had to give up their masks, coppers and other treasures, and many of these ended up in museums. Around the same time, the anthropologist Franz Boas worked for about forty years, starting in the 1880s, with George Hunt, a man raised at Fort Rupert. Together they wrote down thousands of pages about Kwakwaka'wakw language, stories and ceremonies, which families still use today. The ban was quietly dropped in 1951. Kwakwaka'wakw leaders then worked for years to bring the taken treasures home. Many returned, and they are now kept at the U'mista Cultural Centre in Alert Bay, opened in 1980, and at the Nuyumbalees Cultural Centre on Quadra Island.

sections.title: The People Today
sections.text: Today the Kwakwaka'wakw live in a number of First Nations communities on northern Vancouver Island, the nearby islands and the mainland coast, such as Alert Bay, Fort Rupert, Port Hardy, Campbell River and Quadra Island. Many others live in cities like Vancouver and Victoria. Counting them depends on how you count. Band membership across all the Kwakwaka'wakw nations is often given as about 8,000 people. The 2016 Canadian census found about 3,670 people who named Kwakwaka'wakw as their ancestry. Each nation has its own elected or hereditary leaders and runs its own schools, health services, fisheries and businesses. The potlatch has been held openly again since 1951 and is very much alive. Families still gather in big houses to give names, honour the dead, mark marriages and show their dances and masks, with the old songs sung in Kwak'wala. The language itself is in danger, because only a few hundred people learned it as their first language, and most of them are elders. That is why many communities now run language classes, recordings, dictionaries and programs that pair elders with young learners. Some groups use computers and phones to help, which is a good example of how a modern tool can be used to bless and protect something precious. For a Latter-day Saint family, the Kwakwaka'wakw story shows a people who kept their family histories and their love for their ancestors through hard times. That is something many families can honour and understand. When we learn about them, we can do it the way a good guest does at a potlatch: listening carefully, showing respect, and remembering truly what we were shown.

sections.title: Who They Are and Where They Lived About 1500
sections.text: The Coast Salish are many neighboring peoples who live around the Salish Sea, which is the inland water made up of Puget Sound, the Strait of Georgia and the Strait of Juan de Fuca, and up the lower Fraser River. Around the year 1500 they lived in villages along beaches, bays and river mouths, in what is now western Washington and southwestern British Columbia. Their languages belong to the Salishan family. Some of these languages are Lushootseed, spoken around Puget Sound, Halkomelem, spoken by the Musqueam and others along the Fraser River, and Squamish, spoken around Howe Sound and Burrard Inlet. The peoples were not one empire with one ruler. Each village had its own leading families. Villages were tied together by marriage, trade and shared feasts, so a child might have grandparents in two or three different places. Their families had been on the Salish Sea for thousands of years. Their homes were long houses made of cedar planks, and several related families shared one house, each with its own fire. Canoes carved from a single cedar log were their roads, and the sea, rivers and forests gave them almost everything they needed. Many of the place names families still use today come from these old villages.

sections.title: How They Lived and What They Ate
sections.text: Salmon was at the heart of Coast Salish life. Each year, great runs of salmon came home from the ocean to the rivers where they were born. People caught them with weirs, which are fences of wood built across a stream, and with reef nets, a clever method used in the islands near the San Juan and Gulf Islands. In reef netting, a net was stretched between two canoes, and a lookout watched for the fish to swim over it. Salmon was dried and smoked so families could eat it through the winter. People also gathered clams, mussels and other shellfish, and they dug camas bulbs in open meadows and cooked them slowly in earth ovens. In summer they picked berries, and men hunted deer, elk and waterfowl. Women were skilled weavers. They made warm blankets from mountain goat wool and from the soft fur of a special woolly dog that families raised and cared for. Cedar trees gave bark for clothing, baskets, mats and rope, and wood for houses, boxes and canoes. Work followed the seasons: travel to fishing and gathering camps in spring and summer, and staying together in winter villages when the weather turned cold and wet. Sharing food with relatives and guests was a sign of honor.

sections.title: What They Believed About God, Creation, Spirits and the Dead
sections.text: Coast Salish teachings speak of a time long ago when the world was not yet in order. A great figure, often called the Transformer, traveled through the land and changed things into their right shapes. In the stories, he turned some beings into animals, rocks or landmarks, and he set the rules for how people should live. Families still point to rocks and places that are remembered in these stories. The people believed that the whole world is alive with spirit power. Young people went alone into the forest or to the water to fast, bathe and pray, hoping a guardian spirit would come to them and give them a gift, such as skill in fishing, healing or speaking. This power was treated as private and sacred. The people also believed that the salmon, the cedar and the animals are like relatives who give themselves to people, so they must be treated with respect and thanks. The dead were cared for with great love. Families honored them with ceremonies and, in many communities, by burning food and clothing so the departed would be fed and cared for. A parent might gently point out to a child that many peoples have felt that the world was made with order and that the dead are still remembered and loved.

sections.title: Ceremonies and Sacred Things
sections.text: Winter was the season for sacred gatherings. In the longhouse, people who had received spirit power sang their songs and danced, and the whole community came to witness and support them. These winter spirit dances are still held today, and they are private and holy to the families who take part, so visitors should not photograph or record them. In spring and summer, the first salmon of the season was welcomed with a ceremony. It was cooked and shared, and its bones were often returned to the water with care, so that the salmon people would know they had been honored and would come back. Naming feasts were also very important. A family would gather guests, give gifts and pass an old family name to a child or young adult. The guests served as witnesses, helping everyone remember who carried that name and the rights that came with it. Some families among the Musqueam and their Halkomelem-speaking neighbors carry the right to use special masks in certain ceremonies, and that right is handed down within the family. Cedar, songs, names and stories are counted as treasures. Teaching a child to listen quietly and respectfully when sacred things are shared is a good lesson for any family.

sections.title: History Since the First Europeans Came
sections.text: Diseases came before many of the newcomers did. In the late 1700s, smallpox spread through the region and took the lives of a great many people. Spanish and British ships came to these waters in the 1790s, and fur traders followed. The Hudson's Bay Company built Fort Langley on the Fraser River in 1827. In the 1850s, American settlers poured into Puget Sound. Governor Isaac Stevens of Washington Territory made treaties with the tribes. Treaties at Medicine Creek in 1854 and at Point Elliott and Point No Point in 1855 gave up much land, but the tribes kept the right to fish at their usual places. The Point Elliott Treaty was signed on January 22, 1855, by Governor Stevens and by Duwamish Chief Seattle, Snoqualmie Chief Patkanim, Lummi Chief Chow-its-hoot and other leaders. Chief Seattle, or Si'ahl, a leader of the Suquamish and Duwamish, gave his name to the city of Seattle, and he died on the Suquamish Reservation at Port Madison on June 7, 1866. A famous speech is credited to him, but it was printed many years later by a settler from notes, so historians are careful about how much of its wording is his. In the years that followed, many children were sent to boarding and residential schools far from their families and were punished for speaking their language. For a long time, states kept tribes from fishing as their treaties promised. On February 12, 1974, Judge George Boldt ruled that the tribes had a treaty right to half of the salmon and steelhead catch, and that the tribes and the state would manage the fisheries together. In Canada, the Musqueam fisherman Ronald Sparrow's case reached the Supreme Court of Canada, which ruled in 1990 that the Musqueam have an ancestral right to fish.

sections.title: The People Today
sections.text: Today there are dozens of Coast Salish nations in Washington and British Columbia. In Washington they include the Suquamish, Duwamish, Tulalip, Lummi, Swinomish, Muckleshoot, Puyallup, Nisqually, Squaxin Island, Skokomish and several Klallam tribes. In British Columbia they include the Musqueam, Squamish, Tsleil-Waututh, Stó:lō and many nations on Vancouver Island. Many of these nations run their own governments, schools, health clinics, fisheries departments and businesses. They work hard to protect salmon and clean water, because the health of the salmon is tied to the health of the people. Language teachers are bringing back Lushootseed, Halkomelem and Squamish through classes, recordings and dictionaries. The Upper Skagit elder Vi Hilbert spent many years recording Lushootseed and helping others learn it. Since 1989, when canoes paddled to Seattle for Washington's centennial, families have taken part in yearly Canoe Journeys, paddling cedar canoes from village to village and sharing songs, dances and food. In Vancouver, the Musqueam, Squamish and Tsleil-Waututh Nations work together on large land projects in their homelands. Many Coast Salish people are also Christians of different churches, and they hold their faith and their heritage together. For families who believe that Heavenly Father gives people tools to bless one another, it is good to notice how these nations use recordings, schools and new technology to keep old languages alive and to care for the land, while remembering that the same tools can be used to help or to harm.
