sections.title: Who They Are and Where They Lived
sections.text: The Nez Perce call themselves Nimiipuu, which means "the people." The name Nez Perce comes from French and means "pierced nose." French-speaking fur traders gave them that name, though few Nimiipuu ever pierced their noses. Their language, also called Nez Perce, belongs to the Sahaptian family. The Nimiipuu have lived on the high Plateau for thousands of years. Around the year 1500, their homeland was a large country of deep river canyons, green valleys, high meadows and mountains. It covered parts of what are now Idaho, Oregon and Washington. The Snake, Clearwater and Salmon rivers ran through it, and so did the Grande Ronde and Wallowa rivers. The people lived in many small villages along the rivers. Each village had its own leaders, and the leaders listened to the wise older people. Bands that lived near each other were related by marriage and friendship, and they gathered together for fishing, trading and celebrations. A child growing up then would know every river bend, every root field and every mountain trail. Each place had a name and a story. Neighbors such as the Cayuse, Umatilla, Yakama and Palouse traded with the Nimiipuu and often married into their families. Long before Europeans came, trade paths linked the Nimiipuu to the Pacific coast in the west and to the buffalo plains in the east.

sections.title: How They Lived and What They Ate
sections.text: Nimiipuu life followed the seasons. In spring, families dug roots. Camas bulbs grew in wide meadows, and the blue flowers looked almost like lakes. Women used a digging stick to lift the bulbs. They baked them slowly in earth ovens until they turned sweet and dark, and bitterroot and other roots were gathered too. In summer and fall the salmon came up the rivers from the ocean. Men caught them with spears, nets and fish traps, and families dried the fish on racks for winter. Hunters went after deer, elk and mountain sheep, and women picked huckleberries and other berries in the mountains. In winter, families lived together in long lodges built partly into the ground, near the warmer canyon bottoms. Horses reached the Nimiipuu by the early 1700s, and the people became some of the finest horse breeders in North America. They chose their best horses for breeding and traded away the weaker ones. Many of their horses had spotted coats. Settlers later called these horses Appaloosas, a name that likely comes from the Palouse River. Horses let families travel far to hunt buffalo on the plains and to trade. Families who believe Heavenly Father gives new tools so good work can go forward may see the horse as one such gift. It brought food, travel and wealth, but it also brought new contact with distant peoples, along with new conflicts.

sections.title: What They Believed About God, Creation, Spirits and the Dead
sections.text: The Nimiipuu believed in a Creator who made the earth and all living things. They taught that the land, the water, the animals and the plants are alive and must be treated with respect. Many of their old stories tell about a time before people, when animals could talk. The most famous character in those stories is Coyote. Coyote is a trickster. He can be clever and he can be foolish, but he helped get the world ready for human beings. One well-known story tells how a great monster was swallowing all the animals in the Kamiah Valley. Coyote let himself be swallowed and cut the monster's heart from the inside. He then used the monster's body to make the different peoples of the land. He shaped the Nimiipuu last, from the monster's blood, mixed with water. A rock formation near Kamiah, Idaho, is still called the Heart of the Monster, and today it is part of Nez Perce National Historical Park. The Nimiipuu also believed that each person could receive a guardian spirit, called a weyekin. The weyekin often came as an animal or a force of nature, and it gave the person strength, protection and gifts for life. The dead were buried with care, often with some of their belongings. Families mourned openly and honored those who had died, because they believed the spirit went on after the body.

sections.title: Ceremonies and Sacred Things
sections.text: One of the most important moments in a young Nimiipuu life was the vision quest. When a boy or girl was about ten to twelve years old, an elder sent the child alone to a high, quiet place. The child fasted there and waited for a weyekin to appear. Often the child did not tell anyone what the spirit had shown. Its meaning might become clear only years later, in a winter dance where people sang their spirit songs. Another sacred custom was the first-foods feast. Before the people could eat the new salmon, roots or berries of the season, they held a ceremony to give thanks for them. They prayed, sang and served the foods in a set order. Water came first, then salmon, then meat, then roots and berries. This taught children that food is a gift and should not be taken lightly. In the 1800s, many Nimiipuu followed the Washat, also called the Seven Drums religion. It was shared with other Plateau peoples. In Washat worship, seven drummers play while the people sing sacred songs and give thanks to the Creator for the land and its foods. Washat services are still held today. Other Nimiipuu became Presbyterian or Catholic Christians. Many families today keep both their church and the old first-foods teachings close to their hearts.

sections.title: Their History Since the First Europeans Came
sections.text: In September 1805, the explorers Lewis and Clark came out of the Bitterroot Mountains cold and starving. The Nimiipuu fed them on the Weippe Prairie, helped them make canoes, and kept their horses safe until they came back in 1806. In 1831, a small group of Nimiipuu and neighboring men traveled to St. Louis to learn about the white people's teachings, which some called the "Book of Heaven." Missionaries Henry and Eliza Spalding then set up a mission at Lapwai in 1836. In an 1855 treaty, the Nimiipuu kept a large reservation. Then gold was found on their land, and miners and settlers poured in. In 1863 the government made a new treaty that took away most of the reservation. Many bands, including Chief Joseph's band in the Wallowa Valley of Oregon, never signed it and called it the "thief treaty." In 1877 the army ordered these bands onto the small reservation, and fighting broke out. About 800 men, women and children fled for some 1,170 miles across mountains and plains, hoping to reach safety in Canada. At the Bear Paw Mountains in Montana, about forty miles short of the border, Chief Joseph surrendered in October 1877, saying "I will fight no more forever." The people were sent to Kansas and then to Indian Territory, where many died. In 1885 the survivors came back to the Northwest. Some went to Lapwai, and Joseph and his followers went to the Colville Reservation in Washington. Joseph died there in 1904, still far from his beloved Wallowa.

sections.title: The People Today
sections.text: Today most Nimiipuu belong to the Nez Perce Tribe, which has its government center in Lapwai, Idaho. The tribe has several thousand enrolled members and is led by an elected council called the Nez Perce Tribal Executive Committee. Descendants of Chief Joseph's band live on the Colville Reservation in Washington. There they are one of twelve tribes in the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation, and some still gather at Nespelem, where Joseph is buried. The Nez Perce Tribe works hard to care for the land and rivers of its homeland. Its fisheries workers raise and release salmon, and they have helped bring back fish runs that had nearly disappeared. The tribe has also helped restore wolves and other wildlife in Idaho. Young people learn the Nez Perce language in classes and camps, so the words of their grandparents are not lost. Horses still matter: the tribe has run programs that teach youth to raise and ride horses. Every year, families gather for powwows, root feasts and memorial rides that remember the people of 1877. The Nez Perce National Historical Park and the Nez Perce National Historic Trail preserve dozens of places that matter in their story. Families can visit them, and parents can explain to children that these places belonged to a living people. The Nimiipuu are still here, still giving thanks for salmon and camas, and still teaching their children who they are.

sections.title: Who the Ute Are and Where They Lived
sections.text: The Ute call themselves Nuche, which means "the People." Their language, Ute, belongs to the Numic branch of the large Uto-Aztecan family, so it is a cousin of the languages of the Paiute, Shoshone and Comanche. Around the year 1500, long before any European came, the Ute already lived across a huge land of mountains, valleys, deserts and high plateaus. Their homeland covered most of what is now Utah and western Colorado. It also reached into southern Wyoming and the northern edges of Arizona and New Mexico. Utah's Division of State History says this land covered about 225,000 square miles. The People did not live as one big nation with one ruler. They lived in many family groups called bands. These included the Timpanogots by Utah Lake, the Uintah, the Yamparka and Parianuc in the north, the Taviwac (Uncompahgre) in western Colorado, and the Weeminuche, Capote and Muache in the south. Each band chose its own leaders. Still, all the bands were tied together by one language, by marriage, by trade, and by gathering for sacred times such as the Bear Dance. Ute stories say the People have always belonged to these mountains. Scholars think Ute families were using the northern Colorado Plateau one to two thousand years ago. Spanish travellers who met them wrote the name "Yuta," and the word Utah came from that name.

sections.title: How They Lived and What They Ate
sections.text: Ute families moved with the seasons, the way a careful gardener knows when each plant is ready. In spring and summer they went up into the high mountain valleys, where deer and elk grazed and berries ripened. In autumn they gathered pinyon nuts, a rich food from the small pinyon pine, and stored them for winter. Women gathered seeds, roots, berries and greens, and ground the seeds on flat stones. Men hunted deer, elk, antelope, mountain sheep and, on the eastern side of their land, buffalo. Rabbits were caught in drives where many people worked together, and their soft fur was twisted into warm blankets. People near lakes and rivers also fished. Some bands grew corn, beans and squash in small fields. In summer, homes were brush shelters. In colder places they were cone-shaped lodges covered with hides. Ute women were skilled at tanning hides, and later they became famous for fine beadwork on clothing and cradleboards. In the 1600s the Ute were among the first peoples of the Rockies to get horses from the Spanish of New Mexico. The horse was a new tool that changed everything. It let families travel farther, hunt buffalo, and trade widely. Sadly, it also made raiding easier, and some Ute took captives from neighbouring tribes and traded them to the Spanish. Like many tools, the horse could be used to bless or to harm.

sections.title: What They Believed About God, Creation, Spirits and the Dead
sections.text: The Ute have always believed in a Creator. In their stories the Creator is called Sinawav, often written Sinauf in older books. One Ute story, found in Utah histories of the Ute, tells how Sinawav carried the People from the south in a sack and set them down in their mountain home. In these stories Sinawav is wise and good. His younger brother Coyote is clever but foolish and causes trouble, so children learn what happens when people act without thinking. The Ute believed the whole world was alive with power. Mountains, springs, animals, the sun and the weather all had spirit, and people were taught to treat them with respect and give thanks. Some people received special healing power, often through dreams or visions. These medicine people used songs, prayer and plants to help the sick. They were honoured, and they were also expected to use their gift carefully. The Ute believed that a person's spirit lives on after death. Families mourned deeply and buried their loved ones with care, often in rocky places in the hills. In the old days many people avoided saying the name of someone who had died, out of respect and to let the spirit go on its way in peace. When teaching a child, a parent can say that the Ute, like us, believed in a Creator and that life does not end at death.

sections.title: Ceremonies and Sacred Things
sections.text: The oldest and best-loved Ute ceremony is the Bear Dance. Ute tradition says it has been held each spring for as long as anyone can remember. It celebrates the time when bears wake from their winter sleep and the earth begins again, and many Ute think of it as their new year. A story tells of a hunter who met a bear dancing as it came out of its den. The bear taught him the dance and its songs, and asked for respect in return. For several days, families from many bands gather inside a circle of brush. Musicians rub a notched stick to make a deep rumbling sound like a bear's growl, and men and women dance in lines toward each other. It is a time for prayer and for families to meet. Young people make friends there, and some even meet a future husband or wife. The Bear Dance is still held each spring in Ute communities in Utah and Colorado. The Sun Dance came to the Ute from the Shoshone around the 1890s, a hard time when the People had lost much of their land. Dancers fast and pray for several days in a special lodge, asking for healing and for the good of the whole community. The sweat lodge is a small dome where people pray in the steam from heated stones to cleanse body and spirit. Some Ute also belong to the Native American Church, and many are Christians. These ceremonies are sacred, so visitors are asked to follow the tribe's rules, such as not taking photographs.

sections.title: History Since the First Europeans Came
sections.text: Spanish traders from New Mexico met the Ute in the 1600s. In 1776 the Spanish friars Domínguez and Escalante travelled through Ute country and met the Timpanogots by Utah Lake. Later, fur trappers and traders came through on the Old Spanish Trail. When Latter-day Saint pioneers arrived in 1847, they settled in the very valleys where Ute families fished, hunted and gathered. Chief Wakara, also called Walkara or Walker, was a powerful Ute leader who traded horses along the Spanish Trail. He was baptized in 1850 and at first kept an uneasy peace with the settlers. But conflict grew, and the Walker War of 1853 to 1854 brought killings on both sides before Wakara and Brigham Young made peace. Wakara died in 1855. Brigham Young often taught that it was better to feed the Indians than to fight them. Yet settlers still took the best land and water, and many Ute went hungry or died of new diseases. In 1861 President Abraham Lincoln set apart the Uintah Valley Reservation. The Black Hawk War, from 1865 to 1872, began at Manti and was Utah's longest conflict with Native peoples, with deaths and suffering on both sides. Before Black Hawk died in 1870, he visited settlements to make peace. In Colorado there was fighting near the White River agency in 1879. Afterward, the government forced the White River Ute to move to Utah in 1881 and the Uncompahgre Ute in 1882. Later laws opened much reservation land to outsiders, and by 1933 most of the northern Ute lands had been lost.

sections.title: The Ute People Today
sections.text: Today there are three federally recognized Ute tribes. Each has its own elected government, laws, schools and businesses. The Ute Indian Tribe of the Uintah and Ouray Reservation has its headquarters at Fort Duchesne in northeastern Utah. It is made up of the Uintah, White River and Uncompahgre bands, and its reservation is one of the largest in the United States. The tribe runs programs in energy, ranching, education and wildlife, and works to protect its land and water. The Southern Ute Indian Tribe, made up of the Muache and Capote bands, has its home at Ignacio in southwestern Colorado. It is known for carefully managing its natural gas and other businesses, and it supports a cultural centre and museum. The Ute Mountain Ute Tribe, mostly of the Weeminuche band, has its headquarters at Towaoc in southwestern Colorado. It also has lands in New Mexico and in Utah, where the White Mesa community lives. The tribe runs the Ute Mountain Tribal Park, where visitors can see ancient cliff dwellings with Ute guides. In all three tribes, elders and teachers are working hard to keep the Ute language alive, and children learn songs, beadwork and the Bear Dance. Families gather at powwows and spring Bear Dances just as their ancestors did. Ute families belong to many different churches, including The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. They are modern people who also hold on to their own way of life.

sections.title: What Has Been Connected with Israel, the Book of Mormon or a Visiting Teacher
sections.text: There is one real record of a connection, and it comes from Latter-day Saint teaching, not from Ute tradition. Early Latter-day Saints, including Brigham Young and other leaders in the 1840s and 1850s, taught that the Ute and their neighbours were Lamanites, descendants of the people of the Book of Mormon. Because of this belief, missionaries were sent to the Ute and other tribes, and some Ute leaders such as Wakara were baptized. Settlers were urged to treat the Indians as a people of promise. This belief did not prevent hard conflicts over land, and historians remind us that both settlers and Ute suffered. Ute sacred stories do not speak of Israel, of Lehi, or of a visiting teacher. Their own tradition tells of the Creator Sinawav bringing the People to their land. Historians and language scholars trace the Ute to the Numic peoples of the Great Basin. Scholars, including those who study DNA, have found no record linking them to ancient Israel. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints today teaches that the Book of Mormon does not say which modern peoples descend from Lehi. In 2006 the introduction to the Book of Mormon was changed to say the Lamanites are "among the ancestors" of American Indians. The Church's Gospel Topics essay on the Book of Mormon and DNA explains that Lehi's family was likely a small group living among many other peoples. A parent can teach that Heavenly Father loves every people, whatever their ancestry.

card.since: Their ancestors have lived along this coast and these river deltas for thousands of years.
card.lived: Families moved with the seasons. They hunted seals in spring, fished for salmon in summer, picked berries in the fall and gathered other wild foods. Men and older boys lived in a qasgiq, a men's house that was also the village gathering place, while women cared for the children and did the cooking in their own house, called an ena.

card.believed: Yup'ik people taught that animals are aware and must be treated with respect and thanks, or they will not come back to be hunted. They also believed that people's spirits live on after death, so they honored and remembered those who had died.
card.rites: Masked dances were held in the qasgiq, with dancers holding carved dance fans. Winter festivals honored the animals and the dead, among them the Bladder Festival, which thanked the seals, and feasts that remembered loved ones who had passed on.
card.known: Yup'ik and Cup'ik people are known for beautiful carved masks, finely woven grass baskets and dance fans, and for keeping their own language and food-gathering way of life when Russian and later American newcomers came to Alaska.
card.today: Yup'ik and Cup'ik people still live in their homeland in Southwest Alaska. Many families still hunt, fish and gather food, and homes with grandparents, parents and children living together are common. Many Yup'ik people are Christians, and many keep their language, dances and crafts alive.
